BYOS EMAIL PLATFORM MASTER CONTEXT

V5.3 Frozen State → Next Implementation

0. SESSION PURPOSE

This is the authoritative compact context for continuing development of the BYOS Email Platform after completion of V5.3.

Use this together with:

  1. ROADMAP_STATUS.md → current implementation/status state
  2. The real project roadmap → intended product direction
  3. This Master Context → architectural and historical context

These three sources should be treated as the starting context for a fresh development session.

1. PROJECT

Project: BYOS Email Platform

Repository: F:\Codex\byos-email

Current branch: master

Current version: V5.3 COMPLETE / FROZEN

The system is a privacy-focused BYOS email platform where users can connect their own storage and maintain encrypted mail infrastructure.

Core architectural priorities:

  • Privacy
  • Encryption
  • Strong secret isolation
  • Least privilege
  • Storage independence
  • Reliable inbound/outbound mail processing
  • Idempotent outbound delivery
  • DKIM signing
  • Minimal trust boundaries

Do not casually redesign existing architecture.

This architecture is frozen for V5.3.

3. CURRENT SERVICES

There are 11 services:

Host exposure was hardened during V5.3.

Current relevant host bindings:

postfix          127.0.0.1:2525 -> 587
inbound-bridge   0.0.0.0:25
inbound-bridge   127.0.0.1:8085

Postgres, Redis, mail-router, storage-worker, crypto-worker, outbound-worker and Rspamd are no longer unnecessarily published to the host.

4. CRYPTO

packages/crypto-core is a critical frozen component.

Current verified state:

cargo test -p byos-crypto-core --lib
29 passed
0 failed

Important crypto properties:

  • HPKE 0.14
  • X25519
  • AES-GCM 0.10
  • HKDF 0.12
  • SHA-256 / sha2 0.10 + OID
  • RSA 0.9 with PEM support
  • BIP39
  • canonical AAD
  • deterministic DKIM RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signing

Important versions:

rsa = { version = "0.9", features = ["pem"] }
sha2 = { version = "0.10", features = ["oid"] }
hkdf = "0.12"

Do NOT revert these versions or reintroduce ring unless a future task explicitly proves it is necessary.

5. OUTBOUND ENCRYPTION

Outbound messages use:

HPKE
+
AES-GCM
+
canonical AAD

Important invariant:

encryption_iv == envelope nonce

Envelope format:

0x01 || nonce || ciphertext

HPKE format:

0x01 || enc || ciphertext

canonical_aad is currently 29 bytes.

Outbound delivery uses:

outbox_seq
reservation_id
delivery_id

These are intentionally immutable/idempotent pieces of the design.

6. RESERVATION + IDEMPOTENCY

Outbound flow:

prepare
 ↓
outbound_reservations
 ↓
outbox_seq
 ↓
send
 ↓
outbound_queue

Important constraints:

UNIQUE(mailbox_id, outbox_seq)
reservation_id FK
UNIQUE reservation_id in queue
UNIQUE delivery_id

Reservation states:

reserved
consumed
expired

Queue states:

pending
accepted_by_mta
delivered
bounced
expired

Repeated send using the same reservation returns the same delivery_id.

This behavior has already been tested successfully.

7. DKIM

DKIM was completed during V5.3.

Current implementation:

outbound-worker
 ↓
decrypt outbound message
 ↓
lookup mailbox.domain_id
 ↓
lookup domains
 ↓
decrypt encrypted DKIM private key
 ↓
dkim_sign()
 ↓
send_raw()
 ↓
Postfix

DKIM is intentionally performed inside outbound-worker.

It must NOT move to:

API
crypto-worker
frontend
WASM
browser

Current key:

RSA-2048
selector = byos
domain = byos.local

Database stores:

domains.dkim_private_key_enc
domains.dkim_public_key
domains.dkim_selector

Private key is encrypted at rest.

The plaintext private key must never appear in:

logs
API
frontend
WASM
Docker image layers
git
database plaintext

DKIM DEK is supplied only to outbound-worker through:

/run/secrets/byos_dkim_dek

Environment variable contains only the file path:

BYOS_DKIM_DEK_FILE

8. SECRET ISOLATION

Current secret boundaries are intentional.

API

Has only:

outbound_delivery_pk

outbound-worker

Has:

outbound_delivery_sk
byos_dkim_dek
outbound_worker_db_password

crypto-worker

NO secrets

mail-router

NO secrets

postfix

NO BYOS secrets

Never move private keys, delivery SK, DKIM DEK or DB worker passwords into API/frontend/WASM merely for convenience.

9. DATABASE LEAST PRIVILEGE

Outbound worker uses:

outbound_worker_login

which belongs to:

outbound_worker

outbound_worker is:

NOLOGIN
non-superuser

It has only required access to:

outbound_queue
outbound_reservations
delivery_log

plus narrow columns from:

domains
mailboxes

It cannot access:

root_secrets
message_metadata
device_mailbox_access
org_recovery_principals
storage_connections

It also cannot access sensitive mailbox columns:

mailbox_sk_wrapped
mailbox_pk
root_secret_id

Do not broaden these permissions without a concrete architectural requirement.

10. POSTFIX

Postfix is intentionally outbound-safe.

Relevant policy:

mynetworks_style = host

mynetworks =
127/8,
10/8,
172.16/12,
192.168/16

smtpd_recipient_restrictions =
permit_mynetworks,
reject_unauth_destination

Current destination includes:

localhost
byos.local

Do not turn this into an open relay.

The worker talks to:

postfix:25

Successful worker delivery means Postfix accepted the message.

External downstream behavior is separate.

example.com tests can produce a downstream nullMX bounce even after worker/Postfix acceptance. That is not an outbound crypto failure.

14. IMPORTANT V5.3 FREEZE RULE

V5.3 is COMPLETE and FROZEN.

Do NOT:

  • redesign the crypto architecture
  • change HPKE
  • change AES-GCM
  • change canonical AAD

unless the new roadmap stage explicitly requires it.

15. DEVELOPMENT STYLE

Before changing code:

  1. Read the relevant existing implementation.
  2. Read ROADMAP_STATUS.md.
  3. Read the relevant section of the real roadmap.
  4. Determine the smallest change required.
  5. Check dependencies and trust boundaries.
  6. Make minimal changes.
  7. Run targeted tests.
  8. Build only affected services when appropriate.
  9. Verify runtime behavior.
  10. Perform a read-only security/integrity check afterward.
  11. Update ROADMAP_STATUS.md.

Avoid broad refactors.

Do not "clean up" unrelated code while implementing a roadmap feature.

16. CURRENT PROJECT PHILOSOPHY

The system values:

minimal trust
+
least privilege

encrypted data

+

inspect → understand → smallest safe change → test → verify

rather than:

rewrite → rebuild everything → hope

Yes. After reviewing the DeepSeek supervision transcript, I’d rate it about 7/10 as a supervisor.

It did several things very well, but there are a few important security and scope mistakes that I would fix before letting OpenCode execute that prompt.

The biggest positive is that DeepSeek chose the same next stage we established: BYOS Storage Architecture / Step 5. The canonical roadmap explicitly places BYOS immediately after the completed outbound stage and says to start with MinIO, then S3/S3-compatible storage, then Google Drive. The roadmap also makes the provider-neutral abstraction a core requirement.

What DeepSeek did well

1. It correctly adapted the plan to the local laboratory

Its reasoning around the lack of AWS/Google credentials was sensible.

Using:

MinIO → real S3-compatible implementation

and

Google Drive → local mock provider

is a reasonable development strategy. That lets the architecture be developed without pretending that a local Docker environment is a production OAuth environment.

This is particularly good because the roadmap itself says MinIO is the first local implementation and that Google Drive/S3 are planned providers.

2. It understood the importance of a provider abstraction

The proposed interface:

Put / Get / Delete / Head / List

is directionally correct.

That keeps:

mailbox → storage interface → provider

instead of:

mailbox → MinIO

which is exactly the architectural objective of Section 9.

3. It respected a lot of the V5.3 boundaries

DeepSeek repeatedly told OpenCode not to touch:

  • HPKE

  • AES-GCM

  • AAD

  • DKIM

  • outbound pipeline

  • existing tests

  • F-01/F-02/F-03

  • secret isolation

That's exactly the kind of supervision we wanted.

It also made OpenCode perform pre-inspection before coding, which is very good engineering discipline.

4. It included proper verification

The proposed E2E testing around MinIO and the mock Drive was useful.

It also remembered to verify:

  • existing E2E tests

  • storage operations

  • encrypted configuration

  • hardening

  • secret isolation

  • DB permissions

That matches the project's evidence-first philosophy.

Where DeepSeek went wrong

This is where I would be much stricter.

🚨 1. The "disable credential encryption in development" idea is the biggest problem

DeepSeek explicitly proposed:

BYOS_STORAGE_ENCRYPTION_ENABLED=false

and then storing storage credentials in plaintext during local development.

It even described the production path as:

API → storage-worker /internal/encrypt → encrypted config

This is the kind of shortcut I would not approve in your project.

Your whole architecture is built around:

minimal trust + isolated secrets + encrypted sensitive material

and the roadmap explicitly requires storage management, credential rotation and least-privilege storage access.

A better rule would be:

Storage credentials are always encrypted at rest. Local development uses deterministic test credentials or a development secret file, not a plaintext database mode.

That gives you the exact same easy local workflow without introducing a dangerous "plaintext mode" that can accidentally leak into staging or production.

I'd score this as a significant supervisory flaw.

🚨 2. The proposed fixed DEK is not something I would accept

DeepSeek suggested generating a fixed development DEK and even put an example fixed key into the design.

That's unnecessary.

There is a huge difference between:

test fixture secret managed explicitly for tests

and

hardcoded cryptographic key embedded in the development instructions/code path.

Your existing project has gone to considerable lengths to keep secrets isolated. The storage DEK should follow the same discipline.

Better:

/run/secrets/storage_dek

or an explicitly generated local development secret outside source control.

Never:

const DEV_KEY = "..."

That would be an especially bad pattern for a security-focused platform.

🚨 3. The prompt became too large for "Step 5"

This is probably the second-biggest problem.

DeepSeek's prompt starts with storage architecture, but then expands into:

  • database migration

  • storage-worker abstraction

  • encryption endpoint

  • API CRUD

  • Google OAuth

  • Control Plane UI

  • mailbox creation

  • storage assignment

  • mock Drive

  • production Google Drive

  • tests

  • mailbox endpoint

That's a lot.

The canonical roadmap separates these concerns:

  • Section 9: BYOS Storage Architecture

  • Section 10: Customer Experience

  • Section 11: Storage Management Layer

  • Section 1: Organization model

  • Section 3: Control Plane

  • etc.

Some integration is obviously necessary, but DeepSeek blurred the boundaries.

That's risky because OpenCode could turn:

"build the provider abstraction"

into:

"let's build half the storage-management product."

Your philosophy says smallest possible change, and I think DeepSeek should have been more aggressive about limiting scope.

4. "Auto-create a default MinIO connection" is questionable

DeepSeek suggested automatically creating a MinIO storage connection so existing mailboxes continue working.

I don't love this.

Hidden database mutation on application startup creates awkward lifecycle behavior:

start API → magically modify DB

I'd prefer something explicit:

dev bootstrap / migration / seed → create known local MinIO connection

That makes state deterministic and avoids production startup accidentally creating storage resources.

5. Google Drive mock is good, but the production implementation was pushed too early

DeepSeek wanted the codebase to contain:

GoogleDriveStorage

plus

GoogleDriveMockStorage

That's not inherently bad.

But I'd tell OpenCode:

Implement the provider contract and local mock now. Do not implement real Google OAuth until the roadmap stage actually requires it.

Otherwise you're introducing OAuth credentials, callback handling, token storage and another security boundary before they're needed.

The roadmap does eventually require Google Drive, but it also says implementation should proceed in staged order.

One thing DeepSeek did particularly well as a "supervisor"

The approval loop was good.

It went roughly:

inspect → design note → supervisor review → approval → implementation instructions

rather than:

That is exactly the right behavioral model for OpenCode.

The problem is that the supervisor then approved a design containing security shortcuts.
